From spectators gathering for a flag-raising at a new Cenotaph in 1968 to veterans marching to city hall for a Korean War plaque dedication in 1994, Williams Lake has a long tradition of honouring those who served – one that continues. The Williams Lake and District Cenotaph was built in 1968 below the former War Memorial Hospital, a joint undertaking by the municipality and Royal Canadian Legion Branch 139 to honour the area’s war dead, according to the Veterans Affairs Canada’s website. The Cariboo War Memorial Hospital opened in May 1925, partly funded by the community of Soda Creek to honour fallen First World War soldiers. In 1968, the _Williams Lake Tribune_ reported on spectators gathering for a flag-raising ceremony at the new monument. Sixteen years later, the cenotaph was moved beside city hall and rededicated on Nov. 3, 1984, in conjunction with the dedication of the new municipal building. Days after the cenotaph’s rededication beside city hall, the _Tribune’s_ Nov. 8, 1984 edition outlined the plans for that year’s Remembrance Day Observance, bringing together veterans, students and community groups. The service began at 10:45 a.m. at the Elks Hall on Nov. 11, 1984 with the Williams Lake Community Band playing O Canada and a student from Anne Stevenson Junior Secondary School’s drama class reading In Flanders Field. Bill Lannigan and A.E McMath read the names of the former residents who died in the First and Second World Wars, followed by the Last Post and two minutes of silence. items.title: [tsln.com] Cattle specialists urge targeted winter feeding to manage costs
items.content_html:
🌾 ✏️

Cattle advisers and researchers are urging producers to match winter rations to forage quality and herd needs. Drought has tightened forage supplies, and feed is a major operating expense. South Dakota State University research found that limit-fed, energy-dense diets reduced feed use and methane emissions without harming calf growth through weaning, saving about $29 per cow. Kansas State University cow-calf specialist Jason Warner recommends assessing forage and supplementing protein as dormant grasses lose quality. French livestock trainer Guillaume Beaure describes reducing feed waste by closely matching rations to animals’ needs. Advisers also recommend checking forage mineral levels because winter hay can pose a risk of magnesium deficiency.

Risk rises when the hay is also low in calcium and high in potassium, which can interfere with magnesium absorption (tsln.com).

When Paracel arrived in Tacuarita, an Indigenous community of homes made from planks and plastic sheeting in Paraguay’s poorest region, six years ago, it was a welcome sight. The company improved the dirt roads and dug an electric-powered well, saving villagers a two-mile journey to fetch water from a cattle pond that often made them sick. It also gave dozens of local people forestry jobs.

“They fulfilled all their promises,” says Florencio Garcete, 55, chief of the Mbya Guaraní community of 211 people.

items.title: [americanagnetwork.com] USDA cuts corn yield, tightens soybean stocks, lifts grain prices
items.content_html:
🌾 ✏️

The U.S. Department of Agriculture (USDA) cut its 2026/27 U.S. corn yield estimate to 179.6 bushels per acre in its Nov. 10 World Agricultural Supply and Demand Estimates report, lowering projected production by 141 million bushels to 15.893 billion. Soybean yield edged up to 53.3 bushels per acre, but a higher export forecast reduced projected ending stocks by 15 million bushels to 300 million. The tighter-than-expected estimates lifted grain futures: December corn rose nearly 12 cents to $4.51 a bushel, and January soybeans gained more than 35 cents to above $12.24 during Tuesday trading. USDA also lowered its corn export forecast by 25 million bushels and raised its soybean export forecast by the same amount. With most U.S. production estimates now set until USDA’s January update, traders are watching export demand and South American crop weather.

items.title: [ja.se] European farm groups seek exemption from energy rationing during shortages
items.content_html:
🌾 ✏️

Copa-Cogeca, an umbrella group for European farm organizations and cooperatives, has urged the European Commission and EU member states to exempt agriculture and food production from any energy restrictions imposed during a shortage. In a letter sent ahead of an EU energy ministers’ meeting scheduled for Oct. 29, it said farming and food processing depend on reliable supplies of electricity, gas and fuel. The group also called for a coordinated EU approach to high energy and diesel prices, arguing that differing national support measures could distort competition between farmers. It wants better rural grid connections, simpler permits and greater access to financing to help farms produce renewable energy. It also supports greater use of sustainably produced European biofuels to reduce reliance on imported fossil fuels.

items.title: [oglobo.globo.com] El Niño threatens harvests as Peru warns millions face flood risk

An exceptionally strong 2026–27 El Niño is disrupting food production and prompting emergency measures. Peru declared an emergency across more than 70% of its municipalities over flood danger, with authorities warning that more than 9 million people face a high risk of floods and landslides. In the Philippines, unmilled rice production fell 18% in the three months to September, while forecasters expect below-normal rainfall in November. Nearly 896,000 hectares have burned in Indonesia since January; smoke has led to school closures and respiratory illness, according to a report citing BBC. Cereal maker Kellanova has also changed the ingredients in Rice Krispies and Coco Pops sold in the UK and Europe, citing weather-related problems with the availability and quality of rice and grains. The UN’s International Fund for Agricultural Development (IFAD) says overlapping climate and economic shocks could cost the global economy as much as $11 trillion, with energy and fertilizer costs adding pressure across food systems. The UN Food and Agriculture Organization (FAO) said in September it had received only one-fifth of the $202 million requested to prepare for food crises in 22 high-risk countries.

items.title: [eos.org] Arctic ice cores trace century-old toxic pollution to Montana mine
items.content_html:
🌾 ✏️

Researchers traced arsenic and other heavy metals preserved in 10 Arctic ice cores to the Anaconda Copper Mine in Montana, linking pollution to a single industrial source thousands of kilometers away. Arsenic levels in some cores reached about 15 times preindustrial levels around 1914, according to the study in Nature Sustainability. By combining ice-core measurements, atmospheric modeling and historical production records, the team estimated that about 50.5 million Americans and 600,000 Canadians were exposed to arsenic levels associated with increased health risks between 1898 and 1918. Pollution-control equipment installed at the smelter in 1919 reduced emissions by roughly 60% to 65%, though the mine continued operating until 1947. Lead researcher Joseph McConnell, a climate and environmental scientist at the Desert Research Institute, said epidemiologists should investigate the pollution’s potential effects on people.

items.title: [carbonbrief.org] El Niño-linked fires lift total carbon emissions despite fossil fuel dip
items.content_html:
🌾 ✏️

El Niño-related peat fires and forest degradation in Southeast Asia are projected to push land-use carbon emissions higher in 2026, bringing total global CO₂ emissions to 43.3 billion tonnes even as fossil-fuel emissions edge down, according to the Global Carbon Project’s annual assessment. The researchers link the rise in land-use emissions to drier conditions and fires often ignited by human activity. The 21st Global Carbon Budget, published Nov. 10 in Earth System Science Data and presented during the U.N. climate conference in Antalya, projects 5.1 billion tonnes of emissions from land-use change this year. The projected decline in fossil-fuel emissions is partly attributable to the Iran conflict’s energy shock, alongside the growing contribution of solar, wind and electric vehicles. The report says the land carbon sink recovered in 2025 after weakening during the 2023-24 El Niño, but the strong 2026 El Niño is expected to weaken it again in 2027. Separately, an analysis of Chinese data found that emissions fell 3.1% in July-September, the country’s steepest quarterly drop since pandemic lockdowns in 2022.

Officials expected river levels to crest Thursday and then recede. items.content_html:

Full-size 3D-printed tungsten tiles survived 74 plasma discharges inside the DIII-D National Fusion Facility in San Diego, remaining intact after about four minutes of total plasma exposure over three days. The test subjected industrial-scale printed components to conditions relevant to fusion-reactor hardware, including intense heat and particle bombardment. Researchers from North Carolina State University, Oak Ridge National Laboratory and Japanese manufacturer JEOL made the tiles using electron-beam powder bed fusion, keeping the tungsten powder bed above 1,400°C during printing to limit cracking. The parts still await detailed erosion and surface analysis after a radiation survey.

items.title: [sciencedaily.com] Researchers identify heme in 115-million-year-old Brazilian dinosaur fossil
items.content_html:
🌾 ✏️

An international research team says it has found mineralized structures resembling red blood cells and heme, a molecule associated with hemoglobin, in a 115-million-year-old Aratasaurus museunacionali fossil from northeastern Brazil. The team describes the findings, published in the Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences, as the first chemical confirmation of heme-derived molecules inside structures interpreted as dinosaur blood cells. The team says the structures lay inside the bone’s vascular canals and that the surrounding sediment lacked the same heme signature. It proposes that the mineral hausmannite helped preserve the structures and associated molecules; rapid burial in a low-oxygen setting may also have slowed decay. Paleontologist Mary Schweitzer, who was not involved in the study, disputes whether the evidence definitively identifies heme within the cell-like structures, noting that the chemical analysis covered the whole bone. The researchers say fossilization may have distorted the structures’ shape and that further work is needed to interpret it.
